title: Reading an Industry
summary: A case-ready handbook to 12 Indian industries: how each one makes money, the words it uses, the numbers to check, and a worked example for every industry.

chapters.title: How to use this handbook
chapters.markdown:
An **industry** is a group of businesses that make money in the same way: they buy similar inputs, sell to similar customers and worry about the same numbers. Once we know how an industry makes money, any company in it becomes much easier to read.

Cases, interviews and group discussions rarely test whether we know a company. They test whether we can find what drives its profit in the first ten minutes. This handbook gives that head start for 12 industries that come up again and again in Indian cases.

### How each chapter is built

Every industry follows the same seven parts, so we always know where to look:

1. **In one line:** a plain definition of the industry and what makes it different.
2. **How it makes money:** a driver tree that breaks profit into the few numbers that decide it, with a diagram.
3. **Words you will hear:** the jargon, each term with a plain meaning and an everyday example.
4. **Numbers to check:** the ratios analysts look at first, and what each one tells us.
5. **Questions to ask in a case:** a short checklist for the recommendation.
6. **Worked example:** a made-up company with simple numbers, solved step by step.
7. **Where to check the latest:** public sources for current figures.

### How to use it in a case

![Five steps to read any industry in a case](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i00_steps.png)

1. **Step 1, Find the money:** draw the driver tree for the company in the case. It tells us which three or four numbers matter.
2. **Step 2, Learn the words:** read the key terms before the case data, so the exhibits make sense when we reach them.
3. **Step 3, Put numbers on it:** fill the tree with the case figures, or with sensible guesses if the case gives none.
4. **Step 4, Find the lever:** change one number at a time and see which one moves profit most. That is usually the answer.
5. **Step 5, Check before quoting:** industry figures change every quarter, so we check the latest number in a public source before using it.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "A note on the numbers", "icon": "fa-calculator", "text": "Every company in the worked examples is made up, and every number in them is illustrative. They show how the maths works, not what any real company earns."}
```

> **Download the whole handbook:** [Reading an Industry (PDF)](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry.pdf)

chapters.title: Airlines
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

An **airline** sells seats on flights. Its product cannot be stored: an empty seat on a flight that has left is revenue lost forever. Hence the whole industry is about filling seats at a fare above the cost of flying them.

India is one of the world's largest domestic aviation markets, and low-cost carriers (LCCs) carry most of its passengers. Most domestic flights are short, so narrow-body aircraft such as the A320 and 737 families dominate fleets.

### How it makes money

![What decides an airline's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i01_airlines.png)

An airline's capacity is measured in **available seat kilometres (ASK)**: seats on offer multiplied by the distance flown. Revenue is the capacity it sells, multiplied by what each passenger-km earns. Cost is the capacity it flies, multiplied by the cost of flying one seat for one km. Thus profit depends on just three numbers: how many seats are filled, at what fare, and at what cost per seat-km.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Available seat kilometre (ASK)** | One seat flown for one kilometre, the basic unit of capacity. | A 180-seat plane flying 1,000 km offers 1,80,000 ASKs. |
| **Revenue passenger kilometre (RPK)** | One paying passenger flown for one kilometre. | 120 passengers on that 1,000 km flight give 1,20,000 RPKs. |
| **Passenger load factor (PLF)** | RPK ÷ ASK: the share of seats filled. | 1,20,000 ÷ 1,80,000 = 67%. |
| **Yield** | Revenue per RPK: what each passenger pays per kilometre. | A ₹4,500 fare for a 1,000 km trip is a yield of ₹4.5. |
| **RASK and CASK** | Revenue and cost per ASK. Profit per seat-km is RASK minus CASK. | RASK ₹4.3 and CASK ₹4.1 leave ₹0.2 per seat-km. |
| **Breakeven load factor** | CASK ÷ yield: the share of seats an airline must fill just to cover costs. | CASK ₹4.2 ÷ yield ₹4.5 = 93%. |
| **Low-cost carrier (LCC)** | An airline with one cabin class, one aircraft type and quick turnarounds, built to keep CASK low. | Most Indian domestic seats are flown by LCCs. |
| **Hub-and-spoke vs point-to-point** | Flying passengers through a central airport, versus flying them directly between cities. | A Kochi–Delhi–London trip uses a hub; Kochi–Bengaluru is point-to-point. |
| **Wet and dry lease** | Renting an aircraft with crew and maintenance (wet) or the aircraft alone (dry). | Airlines wet-lease planes to cover a short-term gap. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Load factor:** are seats being filled? A falling PLF with rising capacity often means the airline added flights too fast.
2. **RASK minus CASK:** the real profit per seat-km. It strips out the effect of size.
3. **CASK excluding fuel:** shows how efficient the airline itself is, since every airline pays roughly the same for fuel.
4. **Fleet age and utilisation (block hours per day):** older planes burn more fuel; planes that fly more hours a day spread fixed costs further.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. How much of cost is fuel, and how exposed is the airline to oil prices and the rupee? Fuel is often the largest single cost.
2. Is the fleet one aircraft type? One type keeps training, spares and maintenance cheap.
3. Is new capacity entering the routes in the case? Extra seats push fares down for everyone.
4. Are planes grounded (for example, for engine problems)? Grounded aircraft still cost lease rent.

### Worked example: Can a 50-aircraft airline make money?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up LCC has 50 aircraft of 180 seats. Each flies 6 sectors a day of 900 km on average. It fills 85% of seats, earns a yield of ₹4.5 per passenger-km, and its CASK is ₹4.2."}
```

**Step 1, Capacity:** 50 × 180 × 6 × 900 × 365 = about 17.7 billion ASK a year.

**Step 2, Traffic:** 17.7 billion × 85% = about 15.1 billion RPK.

**Step 3, Revenue:** 15.1 billion × ₹4.5 = about ₹6,790 crore.

**Step 4, Cost:** 17.7 billion × ₹4.2 = about ₹7,450 crore.

**Step 5, Result:** a loss of about ₹660 crore, even with 85% of seats full.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "The breakeven load factor is ₹4.2 ÷ ₹4.5 = 93%, which is very hard to reach. Hence the fix is not more passengers: it is a higher yield (better fares on busy routes) or a lower CASK (newer, fuller, more-used aircraft)."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- DGCA monthly domestic traffic data
- Ministry of Civil Aviation
- Airline annual reports and investor presentations

chapters.title: FMCG
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG)** are everyday products that people buy often and cheaply: soap, biscuits, tea, shampoo. Each sale is small, so the industry wins on volume, reach and brand rather than on any single sale.

India's FMCG market sells through a few lakh large stores and many lakh small kirana shops, so distribution is as important as the product. Modern trade (supermarkets) and quick-commerce apps are growing fast in cities, while rural India is a large share of volume.

### How it makes money

![What decides FMCG sales](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i02_fmcg.png)

FMCG sales are simply volume multiplied by price. Volume comes from three things: how many households the product reaches, what share of them buy it, and how often. Profit then depends on the gross margin left after raw materials, minus the large spend on advertising and distribution. Thus a strong FMCG company is usually strong at reach and brand, not just at making the product.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **SKU (stock keeping unit)** | One specific product in one size and variant. | A ₹10 pack and a ₹50 pack of the same biscuit are two SKUs. |
| **Penetration** | The share of households that bought the product at least once in a period. | If 60 of 100 homes bought a brand of tea this year, penetration is 60%. |
| **Distribution reach** | The number of shops that stock the product. | A soap sold in 50 lakh outlets beats a better soap sold in 5 lakh. |
| **General trade vs modern trade** | Traditional kirana shops and wholesalers, versus organised supermarkets and chains. | Most Indian FMCG volume still goes through general trade. |
| **Price-pack architecture** | The ladder of pack sizes and price points a brand offers. | ₹1 and ₹2 shampoo sachets bring in rural buyers. |
| **A&P (advertising and promotion)** | Spending on ads and offers, often 8–15% of sales in FMCG. | Festival-season TV campaigns. |
| **Private label** | A retailer's own brand, usually cheaper than national brands. | A supermarket's own atta brand. |
| **Inventory days** | 365 ÷ (cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory): how long stock waits before it sells. | 61 days of inventory means stock sits for two months. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Volume growth vs price growth:** growth from selling more is healthier than growth from raising prices.
2. **Gross margin:** shows pricing power and exposure to raw materials such as palm oil, wheat or crude-based packaging.
3. **A&P as % of sales:** how hard the company has to push to hold its share.
4. **Rural vs urban growth:** rural demand often moves with crop incomes and the monsoon.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Is growth coming from volume or from price increases?
2. How many outlets does the brand reach, and could a cheaper pack reach more?
3. Which raw materials matter, and can the company pass on cost increases?
4. Is a new channel (quick commerce, modern trade) asking for bigger discounts or longer credit?

### Worked example: How big is the market for a ₹2 shampoo sachet in one state?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up brand wants to launch a ₹2 sachet in a state with 2 crore households. We assume 60% of households use sachets, twice a week."}
```

**Step 1, Users:** 2 crore × 60% = 1.2 crore households.

**Step 2, Sachets a year:** 1.2 crore × 2 a week × 52 weeks = about 125 crore sachets.

**Step 3, Market value:** 125 crore × ₹2 = about ₹250 crore a year.

**Step 4, Our target:** a 5% share would be about ₹12.5 crore of sales.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "The market is large, but each rupee comes in tiny pieces. Hence the plan lives or dies on distribution: how many shops in the state we can reach, and at what cost per shop."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Company annual reports and quarterly results
- IBEF sector reports
- NielsenIQ and Kantar press releases on consumer trends

chapters.title: Retail
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

A **retailer** buys goods from brands and sells them to consumers, earning the gap between the two prices. Margins are thin, so a retailer wins by selling a lot from every square foot and turning stock over quickly.

Indian retail is mostly unorganised: small family shops still sell most goods. Organised chains (grocery, fashion, electronics) and e-commerce are growing, and many retailers now sell both in stores and online.

### How it makes money

![What decides a store's sales](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i03_retail.png)

Store sales are footfall × conversion × average bill. Dividing by floor area gives **sales per square foot**, the number that tells us whether a store pays for its rent. Profit then depends on the gross margin earned on goods, minus rent, staff and power. Thus a good location only pays off if the store also converts visitors and keeps stock moving.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Footfall** | The number of people who enter a store. | 1,500 visitors a day. |
| **Conversion rate** | The share of visitors who buy something. | 450 bills from 1,500 visitors is 30%. |
| **Average transaction value (ATV)** | The average bill size. | ₹800 per bill. |
| **Sales per square foot** | Sales ÷ selling area, usually per month. | ₹1,100 per sq ft per month. |
| **Same-store (like-for-like) growth** | Growth from stores open more than a year, which strips out new openings. | A chain growing 20% overall but 2% like-for-like is growing only by opening stores. |
| **Shrinkage** | Stock lost to theft, damage or errors. | 1% of sales lost each year. |
| **Omnichannel** | Selling through stores, website and app as one business. | Order online, pick up in store. |
| **GMV vs net revenue** | The total value of goods sold on a platform, versus what the platform keeps as revenue. | A marketplace with ₹100 crore GMV and a 15% commission has ₹15 crore of revenue. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Same-store sales growth:** is the existing business healthy, or is growth bought with new stores?
2. **Sales per sq ft and rent per sq ft:** rent as a share of sales shows whether a location works.
3. **Inventory turnover:** how quickly stock sells; fashion and electronics lose value if they sit.
4. **Store payback period:** how many years a new store takes to earn back its fit-out cost.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Is the problem footfall, conversion or bill size? Each needs a different fix.
2. What share of sales goes on rent, and is the lease fixed or linked to sales?
3. How much stock is old or slow-moving?
4. Does online growth add new customers, or move existing ones from stores?

### Worked example: Does a 10,000 sq ft store cover its rent?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up grocery store of 10,000 sq ft gets 1,500 visitors a day, converts 30% of them, and the average bill is ₹800. Rent is ₹150 per sq ft per month."}
```

**Step 1, Bills a day:** 1,500 × 30% = 450.

**Step 2, Sales a year:** 450 × ₹800 × 365 = about ₹13.1 crore.

**Step 3, Sales per sq ft per month:** ₹13.1 crore ÷ 12 ÷ 10,000 = about ₹1,095.

**Step 4, Rent share:** ₹150 ÷ ₹1,095 = about 14% of sales.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Grocery earns a thin gross margin, so 14% of sales going on rent leaves little for staff, power and profit. Hence we would test the three levers: renegotiate rent, lift conversion with better availability, or raise the average bill with higher-margin ranges."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Company annual reports
- IBEF retail reports
- Retailers Association of India (RAI) publications

chapters.title: Banking
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

A **bank** borrows money cheaply from depositors and lends it at a higher rate. Its profit is the gap between the two, minus running costs and the loans that go bad.

Indian banks are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). They include public sector banks, private banks, small finance banks and payments banks. Banks must keep part of their deposits as cash reserves (CRR) and in safe assets such as government bonds (SLR), which limits how much they can lend.

### How it makes money

![What decides a bank's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i04_banking.png)

A bank earns **net interest income (NII)**: interest from loans and bonds minus interest paid on deposits. Dividing NII by average assets gives the **net interest margin (NIM)**. Add fee income, subtract operating costs and provisions for bad loans, and what is left is profit. Thus a bank does well when it has cheap deposits, lends at a good rate, and keeps bad loans low.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Net interest margin (NIM)** | Net interest income ÷ average interest-earning assets. | ₹4,000 crore of NII on ₹1,00,000 crore of assets is a NIM of 4%. |
| **CASA ratio** | Current and savings account deposits as a share of all deposits. These pay little or no interest. | A bank with 40% CASA has cheaper funds than one with 25%. |
| **Gross and net NPA** | Loans overdue by 90 days or more (gross), and the same after setting aside provisions (net). | A GNPA of 3% means 3 of every 100 rupees lent are in trouble. |
| **Provision coverage ratio (PCR)** | Provisions held ÷ gross NPAs: how much of the bad loans is already written off in the books. | A PCR of 75% means only a quarter of the loss is still to come. |
| **Capital adequacy ratio (CRAR)** | Capital ÷ risk-weighted assets. The RBI sets a minimum so banks can absorb losses. | Riskier loans need more capital behind them. |
| **CRR and SLR** | The share of deposits a bank must keep with the RBI as cash (CRR) and in safe liquid assets (SLR). | Money held for CRR earns no interest, so it lowers NIM. |
| **Credit cost** | Provisions for bad loans ÷ average loans. | A credit cost of 1% on ₹70,000 crore of loans is ₹700 crore. |
| **ROA and ROE** | Profit ÷ assets, and profit ÷ shareholders' equity. | For banks, an ROA above 1% is generally seen as healthy. |

### Numbers to check

1. **NIM:** the core earning power of the bank.
2. **CASA ratio:** the cheapest way to a higher NIM.
3. **Gross NPA and credit cost:** the quality of lending, and how much of it is turning into losses.
4. **Cost-to-income ratio:** operating costs ÷ (NII + fees): how efficiently the bank runs.
5. **CRAR:** how much room the bank has to grow before it needs new capital.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Where is loan growth coming from, and is it riskier (unsecured personal loans, credit cards) than before?
2. Is the bank's CASA share rising or falling as interest rates change?
3. Are bad loans concentrated in one sector or region?
4. Does the bank have enough capital to grow, or will it need to raise more?

### Worked example: What happens to a bank's profit if bad loans double?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up bank has ₹1,00,000 crore of assets including ₹70,000 crore of loans. It earns 8.5% on assets and pays 5% on ₹90,000 crore of deposits. Fees are ₹1,000 crore, costs ₹2,000 crore, and credit cost is 1% of loans. Tax is 25%."}
```

**Step 1, Net interest income:** ₹8,500 crore − ₹4,500 crore = ₹4,000 crore, a NIM of 4%.

**Step 2, Before provisions:** ₹4,000 + ₹1,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹3,000 crore.

**Step 3, Provisions:** 1% × ₹70,000 crore = ₹700 crore, so profit before tax is ₹2,300 crore.

**Step 4, Profit:** ₹2,300 crore × 75% = about ₹1,725 crore, an ROA of about 1.7%.

**Step 5, If credit cost doubles to 2%:** provisions rise to ₹1,400 crore, profit before tax falls to ₹1,600 crore and profit to ₹1,200 crore.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "A one-point rise in credit cost cuts profit by about 30%. Hence, in a bank case, the quality of new lending usually matters more than how fast the loan book grows."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- RBI Financial Stability Report
- RBI Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)
- Bank annual reports and investor presentations

chapters.title: NBFCs
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

A **non-banking financial company (NBFC)** lends money like a bank but does not hold a banking licence. Most NBFCs cannot take deposits, so they borrow from banks and bond markets, which makes their money more expensive.

NBFCs are regulated by the RBI and often serve customers banks find harder to reach: vehicle buyers, small businesses, gold-loan borrowers and microfinance groups. Because they rely on borrowed money, a rise in interest rates or a scare in bond markets hits them faster than banks.

### How it makes money

![What decides an NBFC's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i05_nbfc.png)

An NBFC earns the **spread** between what borrowers pay and what it pays its own lenders, on its loan book (**assets under management, AUM**). From that it pays for branches and collections, and sets aside money for bad loans. Since its funds are dearer than a bank's, an NBFC must either charge more, run leaner, or know its customers better to keep losses low.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Deposit-taking vs non-deposit-taking** | A few NBFCs may accept public deposits under strict RBI rules; most may not. | A non-deposit-taking NBFC funds itself with bank loans and bonds. |
| **AUM (assets under management)** | The total loans an NBFC has outstanding. | ₹10,000 crore of vehicle loans. |
| **Disbursement** | New loans paid out in a period. | ₹500 crore of new two-wheeler loans in a quarter. |
| **Spread** | Yield on loans minus cost of borrowing. | 14% − 9% = 5 percentage points. |
| **ALM mismatch** | Asset-liability mismatch: lending for long periods with money borrowed for short ones. | Funding five-year home loans with 90-day commercial paper is risky. |
| **Co-lending** | A bank and an NBFC sharing a loan: the bank brings cheap money, the NBFC brings the customer. | A bank funds 80% of a small-business loan sourced by an NBFC. |
| **Microfinance** | Small, usually unsecured loans to low-income borrowers, often through groups. | ₹30,000 loans to women's self-help groups. |
| **Risk weight** | How much capital the RBI asks a lender to hold against a type of loan. | Raising risk weights on unsecured loans makes them costlier to give. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Spread and NIM:** the margin the business runs on.
2. **Cost of borrowing and credit rating:** a better rating means cheaper money.
3. **Gross stage 3 / NPA and credit cost:** how well the NBFC chooses and collects from borrowers.
4. **AUM growth vs disbursement growth:** fast growth in risky segments can hide problems for a year or two.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. How is the NBFC funded, and for how long? Short-term funds for long-term loans is a warning sign.
2. Which customer segment does it serve, and what happens to that segment in a downturn?
3. Is it growing faster than its collection team can handle?
4. Would co-lending with a bank lower its cost of funds?

### Worked example: How sensitive is an NBFC to borrowing costs?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up vehicle-finance NBFC has ₹10,000 crore of loans, funded by ₹8,000 crore of borrowings at 9% and ₹2,000 crore of equity. Loans yield 14%. Operating costs are 3% of AUM and credit cost 2%. Tax is 25%."}
```

**Step 1, Interest earned:** 14% × ₹10,000 crore = ₹1,400 crore.

**Step 2, Interest paid:** 9% × ₹8,000 crore = ₹720 crore, so net interest income is ₹680 crore.

**Step 3, Costs:** ₹300 crore operating cost and ₹200 crore credit cost leave ₹180 crore before tax.

**Step 4, Profit:** ₹180 crore × 75% = ₹135 crore, an ROE of about 6.8%.

**Step 5, If borrowing costs rise by 1 point:** interest paid rises by ₹80 crore, and profit before tax falls from ₹180 crore to ₹100 crore.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "A one-point rise in funding cost removes almost half the profit. Hence, for an NBFC, how it borrows is as important as whom it lends to."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- RBI reports on NBFCs (Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India)
- Credit rating agency reports (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE)
- NBFC annual reports

chapters.title: IT services
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

An **IT services company** sells the time and skills of its engineers to clients, mostly abroad. It earns in dollars and euros and pays salaries in rupees, so its profit depends on keeping people busy on billable work.

India is one of the world's largest exporters of IT and business process services, and most revenue comes from clients in North America and Europe. Work is shifting from maintaining old systems towards cloud, data and AI projects.

### How it makes money

![What decides IT services revenue](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i06_it.png)

For time-and-material work, revenue is headcount × utilisation × billable hours × rate. The main cost is salaries. Margins move with **utilisation** (how much paid time is billed), the **pyramid** (how many juniors per senior), the **offshore mix** (work done in India is cheaper) and the rupee. Thus an IT company makes money by keeping the right people busy on work clients value.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Utilisation** | Billed hours ÷ available hours of billable staff. | An engineer billed 32 of 40 hours a week is 80% utilised. |
| **Bench** | Employees between projects, paid but not billed. | A large bench lowers margins. |
| **Attrition** | The share of employees who leave in a year. | 20% attrition means hiring and training one in five people again. |
| **Pyramid** | The ratio of junior to senior staff. A wider base lowers average cost. | Five freshers for every project manager. |
| **Onsite vs offshore** | Work done at the client's site abroad, versus in India. Offshore is cheaper. | 70% offshore effort is a common target. |
| **Time-and-material vs fixed-price** | Billing for hours worked, versus a fixed fee for a defined result. | Fixed-price deals reward efficiency but carry overrun risk. |
| **Deal TCV** | Total contract value of new deals signed: a lead indicator of future revenue. | A $500 million five-year deal. |
| **Constant-currency growth** | Growth with exchange-rate effects removed. | Revenue up 8% in rupees but 4% in constant currency. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Constant-currency revenue growth:** real demand, without currency noise.
2. **EBIT margin:** the combined result of utilisation, pyramid, offshore mix and wage hikes.
3. **Utilisation and attrition:** today's efficiency and tomorrow's hiring cost.
4. **Deal wins (TCV) and top-client concentration:** how secure future revenue is.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Which industries do the company's clients come from, and are they cutting tech budgets?
2. Is new work in growing areas (cloud, data, AI) or in shrinking ones?
3. What happens to margins after the yearly wage hike?
4. How much revenue comes from the top 10 clients?

### Worked example: How much does a drop in utilisation cost?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up firm has 1,000 billable engineers, each available for 1,800 hours a year, billed at $30 an hour. Utilisation is 80%. We take $1 = ₹85. Salaries are ₹150 crore and other costs ₹140 crore."}
```

**Step 1, Billed hours:** 1,000 × 1,800 × 80% = 14.4 lakh hours.

**Step 2, Revenue:** 14.4 lakh × $30 = $43.2 million, or about ₹367 crore.

**Step 3, Profit:** ₹367 crore − ₹290 crore = about ₹77 crore, a margin of 21%.

**Step 4, At 75% utilisation:** revenue falls to about ₹344 crore while costs stay the same, so profit falls to about ₹54 crore, a margin of 16%.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Five points of utilisation take away five points of margin, because salaries are paid whether or not hours are billed. Hence managing the bench is one of the most important jobs in an IT company."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- NASSCOM strategic reviews
- Company quarterly results and investor presentations
- RBI data on services exports

chapters.title: Automobile
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

An **automobile maker (OEM)** designs and assembles vehicles from thousands of parts made by suppliers, and sells them through dealers. Plants are expensive and costs are largely fixed, so volume decides profit.

India is one of the world's largest vehicle markets and the largest for two-wheelers. The industry includes two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles and tractors, each with its own demand drivers. Emission rules (BS-VI) and the shift to electric vehicles are changing what gets built.

### How it makes money

![What decides an auto maker's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i07_auto.png)

Revenue is vehicles sold × average **realisation** per vehicle. Raw materials are the biggest variable cost. A large share of the rest (plants, R&D, staff) is fixed, so profit is very sensitive to **capacity utilisation**. Thus the same company can swing from loss to strong profit with a 15–20% change in volume.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **OEM** | Original equipment manufacturer: the company whose brand is on the vehicle. | A car maker, as opposed to its tyre or seat supplier. |
| **Wholesale vs retail sales** | Vehicles sent from the factory to dealers, versus vehicles sold by dealers to customers. | Wholesales far above retail means stock is piling up at dealers. |
| **Dealer inventory days** | How many days of sales are sitting at dealers. | 45 days of stock before a festival is normal; after it, a warning. |
| **Realisation per vehicle** | Net revenue ÷ vehicles sold. | Rising when buyers move to SUVs. |
| **Segments** | Two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles and tractors, each with different buyers. | Truck demand follows freight and infrastructure; tractor demand follows farm income. |
| **Platform** | A shared base (chassis and parts) used for several models to save cost. | One platform for a hatchback, a sedan and a compact SUV. |
| **BS-VI** | India's current emission standard, in force since April 2020. | It raised the cost of engines and exhaust systems. |
| **EV and PLI** | Electric vehicles, and the government's production-linked incentive scheme for making them and their parts in India. | Battery cost is the largest part of an EV's price. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Volume growth by segment:** demand and share, segment by segment.
2. **EBITDA margin and EBITDA per vehicle:** pricing power and cost control.
3. **Capacity utilisation:** how close the company is to its operating-leverage sweet spot.
4. **Dealer inventory:** whether reported sales are real demand or stock pushed to dealers.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Which segment is the case about, and what drives its demand (incomes, freight, farm output)?
2. How will the shift to EVs change costs, suppliers and the dealer model?
3. Is the company raising prices faster than raw material costs?
4. Are plants running full, or is there spare capacity to fill?

### Worked example: Why does profit jump when volumes rise?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up two-wheeler maker sells 7 lakh units a year at a realisation of ₹70,000. Variable cost is ₹56,000 per unit and fixed costs are ₹600 crore a year."}
```

**Step 1, Contribution per unit:** ₹70,000 − ₹56,000 = ₹14,000.

**Step 2, At 7 lakh units:** 7 lakh × ₹14,000 = ₹980 crore, minus ₹600 crore fixed = ₹380 crore profit.

**Step 3, At 8 lakh units:** 8 lakh × ₹14,000 = ₹1,120 crore, minus ₹600 crore = ₹520 crore profit.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Volume rose 14%, but profit rose 37%. This is operating leverage, and it works in reverse too. Hence in auto cases we always ask what happens to profit if demand falls by 10–15%."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- SIAM monthly sales data
- FADA retail sales data
- Company annual reports and monthly sales releases

chapters.title: Cement
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Cement** is a heavy, low-value product used in every building, road and bridge. It costs a lot to move, so markets are regional, and the winners are those with low costs close to their customers.

India is the world's second-largest cement producer, after China. Demand follows housing and infrastructure spending. The industry has been consolidating, with the largest groups adding capacity and buying smaller players.

### How it makes money

![What decides a cement company's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i08_cement.png)

Analysts look at a cement company per tonne: realisation per tonne minus cost per tonne gives **EBITDA per tonne**, and multiplying by tonnes sold gives total EBITDA. **Power and fuel** (coal, pet coke) and **freight** are the two largest costs, so plant location matters as much as plant size. Thus a cheap plant far from its market can lose to a dearer one next door.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Clinker** | The intermediate product made by heating limestone in a kiln, then ground with gypsum to make cement. | Clinker making uses most of the energy. |
| **MTPA** | Million tonnes per annum, the unit of capacity. | A 5 MTPA plant can make 50 lakh tonnes a year. |
| **Blended cement** | Cement that replaces some clinker with fly ash (PPC) or slag (PSC). Cheaper and lower in carbon. | Most cement sold in India is blended. |
| **EBITDA per tonne** | Operating profit per tonne sold, the industry's key measure. | ₹1,000 per tonne. |
| **Lead distance** | The average distance from plant to customer. | A 300 km lead costs far more than a 100 km one. |
| **Split grinding unit** | A grinding unit placed near customers, fed with clinker from a distant kiln. | It cuts freight on the heavier finished cement. |
| **Trade vs non-trade sales** | Sales through dealers to home builders, versus direct sales to builders and government projects. | Trade sales usually earn a higher price. |
| **Waste heat recovery (WHR)** | Using hot kiln gases to generate power. | It lowers power cost per tonne. |

### Numbers to check

1. **EBITDA per tonne:** the single best measure of a cement business.
2. **Capacity utilisation:** high fixed costs mean utilisation drives profit.
3. **Power and fuel cost per tonne:** exposure to coal and pet coke prices.
4. **Freight cost per tonne and lead distance:** how well plants sit next to markets.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Which region is the plant in, and how much new capacity is coming there?
2. How far is the plant from limestone, from coal and from customers?
3. Can the company use more blended cement, waste heat or renewable power to cut cost?
4. Is demand driven by housing (trade) or government projects (non-trade)?

### Worked example: What does one plant earn?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up 5 MTPA plant runs at 70% utilisation and realises ₹5,500 per tonne. Costs per tonne are: power and fuel ₹1,400, freight ₹1,300, raw materials ₹900, other ₹900."}
```

**Step 1, Volume:** 5 MTPA × 70% = 3.5 million tonnes.

**Step 2, Cost per tonne:** ₹1,400 + ₹1,300 + ₹900 + ₹900 = ₹4,500.

**Step 3, EBITDA per tonne:** ₹5,500 − ₹4,500 = ₹1,000.

**Step 4, EBITDA:** 3.5 million × ₹1,000 = ₹350 crore.

**Step 5, If customers are 200 km further away:** at an assumed ₹2 per tonne per km, freight rises by ₹400 and EBITDA per tonne falls to ₹600.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Moving the same cement further cuts profit by 40%. Hence cement companies build grinding units near cities and fight hardest for the markets closest to their plants."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) data
- Company quarterly results (volumes, realisation and cost per tonne)
- Rating agency sector reports

chapters.title: Paints
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Paints and coatings** protect and decorate surfaces. In India, most of the market is **decorative** paint for homes, sold through dealers and applied by painters, so brand, dealer reach and painter loyalty matter as much as the product.

Decorative paint makes up most of the Indian market; industrial coatings (for cars, appliances and machinery) are the rest. Several large groups have entered the decorative market recently, adding capacity and pressure on prices and dealer incentives.

### How it makes money

![What decides a paint company's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i09_paints.png)

Revenue is volume × price, with **mix** (premium versus economy paint) making a big difference. Raw materials, many of them linked to crude oil (solvents, monomers) plus titanium dioxide, take more than half of sales. Thus gross margin rises and falls with crude prices, and the strongest brands are those that can raise prices without losing dealers.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Decorative vs industrial paint** | Paint for buildings, versus coatings for products such as cars and machines. | A wall emulsion versus an automotive primer. |
| **Emulsion and enamel** | Water-based paint for walls, versus solvent-based paint for wood and metal. | Emulsion for the living room, enamel for the gate. |
| **Tinting machine** | A machine at the dealer that mixes base paint with colour on the spot. | It lets a dealer offer thousands of shades without holding them in stock. |
| **Dealer network** | The shops that sell the paint. More dealers with tinting machines means more reach. | A company with 1 lakh dealers versus one with 30,000. |
| **Painter programmes** | Loyalty schemes for painters, who often choose the brand for the customer. | Points and training for painters. |
| **VOC** | Volatile organic compounds: chemicals that evaporate from some paints and pollute indoor air. | Low-VOC paints are sold as healthier. |
| **Titanium dioxide (TiO2)** | The white pigment that gives paint its covering power, and a major cost. | A rise in TiO2 prices hits gross margin. |
| **Repainting cycle** | How often homes are repainted, the main source of demand. | A shorter cycle means more volume. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Volume growth vs value growth:** if value grows slower than volume, buyers are moving to cheaper ranges.
2. **Gross margin:** how well price increases keep up with raw material costs.
3. **Number of dealers and tinting machines:** reach, the real moat in decorative paint.
4. **Receivable days:** how much credit the company gives dealers to win shelf space.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. How exposed is the company to crude oil and TiO2 prices, and how quickly can it pass on increases?
2. What does a new entrant offer dealers, and can the incumbent match it?
3. Is demand coming from new housing or from repainting?
4. Is the company selling more premium paint, or trading customers down?

### Worked example: How much must prices rise when raw materials get dearer?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up paint company has ₹1,000 crore of sales. Raw materials cost ₹550 crore (55% of sales), so gross profit is ₹450 crore. Raw material prices rise by 10%."}
```

**Step 1, New raw material cost:** ₹550 crore × 1.10 = ₹605 crore.

**Step 2, To keep gross profit at ₹450 crore:** sales must reach ₹1,055 crore, a price rise of 5.5%.

**Step 3, To keep the gross margin at 45%:** sales must reach ₹605 crore ÷ 55% = ₹1,100 crore, a price rise of 10%.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Hence a paint company facing a 10% rise in raw materials needs at least a 5.5% price increase just to stand still in rupees. If a new entrant is offering dealers lower prices, even that may be hard to pass on."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Company annual reports and quarterly results
- IBEF chemicals and paints reports
- Rating agency sector reports

chapters.title: Oil and gas
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **oil and gas** industry finds and produces crude oil and gas (**upstream**), moves and refines it (**midstream**), and sells fuels to customers (**downstream**). Each stage earns money in a different way, so we always ask which stage the case is about.

India imports most of the crude oil it uses, which makes it one of the world's largest crude importers and a large refiner. Retail fuel prices, taxes and import costs all matter to the economy, so government policy plays a big role in the industry.

### How it makes money

![Three businesses, three profit engines](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i10_oil.png)

Upstream companies earn the crude price minus the cost of getting oil out of the ground. Refiners earn the **gross refining margin (GRM)**: the value of the fuels they make minus the cost of the crude. Fuel retailers earn a margin per litre sold. Thus a rise in crude prices helps a producer, can squeeze a refiner, and may hurt a retailer if pump prices do not follow.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Upstream, midstream, downstream** | Exploration and production; transport and storage; refining and selling. | An oil field, a pipeline, a petrol pump. |
| **Brent** | A benchmark crude oil price used to price most of the world's oil. | News reports quote Brent in dollars per barrel. |
| **Barrel** | The unit for crude oil: about 159 litres. One tonne of crude is roughly 7.3 barrels. | A 10 MMTPA refinery processes about 7.3 crore barrels a year. |
| **GRM (gross refining margin)** | Value of refined products minus crude cost, per barrel. | A GRM of $6 a barrel. |
| **Crack spread** | The price gap between one fuel (diesel, petrol) and crude. | A high diesel crack lifts GRMs. |
| **MMTPA** | Million metric tonnes per annum, the unit of refinery capacity. | A 10 MMTPA refinery. |
| **Reserve replacement ratio** | New reserves found ÷ oil and gas produced in a year. | Below 100% means reserves are shrinking. |
| **City gas distribution (CGD)** | Piping natural gas to homes (PNG) and selling it to vehicles (CNG) in a city. | A city's CNG stations and kitchen gas lines. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Crude price and the rupee:** the starting point for every part of the chain in India.
2. **GRM:** the health of the refining business.
3. **Marketing margin per litre:** what fuel retailers make at the pump.
4. **Production volumes and reserve replacement:** whether an upstream company is growing or running down.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Which part of the chain is the case about: producing, refining or selling?
2. What happens to profit if crude rises by $10 a barrel?
3. How much is decided by government policy (taxes, pricing, subsidies)?
4. How will electric vehicles and cleaner fuels change demand over ten years?

### Worked example: What is a refinery's margin worth?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up 10 MMTPA refinery runs at full capacity. Its GRM is $6 a barrel. We take $1 = ₹85."}
```

**Step 1, Barrels a year:** 10 million tonnes × 7.33 = about 73 million barrels.

**Step 2, Gross margin:** 73 million × $6 = about $440 million, or about ₹3,740 crore.

**Step 3, If GRM falls to $4:** the gross margin falls to about $293 million, a drop of a third.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "A refinery's fixed costs do not move with GRM, so a $2 swing changes profit far more than a third. Hence refiners invest in complex units that turn cheaper, heavier crude into high-value fuels."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) data
- Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
- Company annual reports

chapters.title: Mining and metals
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Mining** digs ores and minerals out of the ground; **metals** companies turn them into steel, aluminium, copper and zinc. Metals are commodities priced globally, so a company cannot set its own price: it wins by having the lowest cost.

India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer and has large reserves of iron ore, coal and bauxite. Demand follows construction, infrastructure and manufacturing, and prices follow global cycles, especially demand from China.

### How it makes money

![What decides a steel maker's profit](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i11_metals.png)

A metals company earns the gap between a price it does not control and a cost it does. For steel, the biggest costs are **iron ore** and **coking coal**, so companies with their own (captive) mines have a lasting cost advantage. Thus we read a metals company by its **EBITDA per tonne** through the cycle, not by one good year.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Ferrous vs non-ferrous** | Iron-based metals (iron, steel), versus others (aluminium, copper, zinc, lead). | A steel plant versus a copper smelter. |
| **Integrated steel plant** | A plant that makes iron from ore in a blast furnace and then steel (BF-BOF). | Large coastal and eastern plants. |
| **Electric arc furnace (EAF)** | A furnace that melts scrap or sponge iron with electricity. Smaller and lower in carbon. | Mini steel plants. |
| **Captive mine** | A mine owned by the company that uses its output. | A steel maker with its own iron ore mine. |
| **Grade** | The share of useful metal in an ore. | Iron ore with 62% iron content. |
| **Stripping ratio** | Waste rock removed ÷ ore extracted in open-cast mining. | A ratio of 3 means three tonnes of waste for every tonne of ore. |
| **LME** | The London Metal Exchange, where prices for aluminium, copper and zinc are set. | Aluminium makers quote LME prices. |
| **Commodity cycle** | The repeated rise and fall of prices as supply catches up with demand. | New capacity added in good years causes the next slump. |

### Numbers to check

1. **EBITDA per tonne over several years:** earning power through the cycle.
2. **Cost per tonne vs peers:** where the company sits on the global cost curve.
3. **Share of captive raw materials:** protection when ore and coal prices rise.
4. **Net debt to EBITDA:** whether the company can survive a downturn.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Where are we in the commodity cycle, and how much new capacity is coming?
2. How much of its ore and coal does the company own?
3. Is it on the coast (cheaper imported coal and exports) or near the mines?
4. How will carbon rules (and carbon taxes on exports to Europe) change its costs?

### Worked example: What is a captive iron ore mine worth?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up steel maker sells 5 million tonnes a year at ₹55,000 per tonne. Each tonne needs 1.6 tonnes of iron ore at ₹5,000 and 0.8 tonnes of coking coal at ₹20,000. Other conversion costs are ₹19,000 per tonne."}
```

**Step 1, Raw material cost:** 1.6 × ₹5,000 + 0.8 × ₹20,000 = ₹24,000 per tonne.

**Step 2, Total cost:** ₹24,000 + ₹19,000 = ₹43,000 per tonne.

**Step 3, EBITDA:** ₹55,000 − ₹43,000 = ₹12,000 per tonne, or ₹6,000 crore a year.

**Step 4, With a captive mine at ₹3,000 a tonne of ore:** the company saves 1.6 × ₹2,000 = ₹3,200 per tonne, lifting EBITDA per tonne by about 27%.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "Hence, in a metals case, owning raw materials is often the real competitive advantage. When steel prices fall, the company with the captive mine still makes money while others make losses."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines annual reports
- Joint Plant Committee (JPC) steel data
- World Steel Association statistics

chapters.title: Alcoholic beverages
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **alcoholic beverages** industry makes and sells spirits, beer and wine. In India it is one of the most regulated consumer industries: each state sets its own taxes, prices and rules on how alcohol is sold.

Alcohol for drinking is outside GST, so states charge excise duty and other levies, and these are a major source of state revenue. Rules on pricing, licences and retail differ by state, and direct advertising of alcohol is not allowed. Indian whiskies are winning international awards, and many consumers are moving to premium brands.

### How it makes money

![Where the money in a bottle goes](content/prep/files/reading-an-industry/i12_alcobev.png)

A large share of what the customer pays goes to the state as taxes, and another share to the trade. The company keeps its **net realisation**, and from that pays for spirit, glass, packaging and marketing. Since prices are often fixed or approved by the state, the main levers are selling more **premium** brands (which earn more per case) and keeping costs such as glass and grain under control.

### Words you will hear

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Case** | The industry's unit of volume: 9 litres, or 12 bottles of 750 ml. | A brand selling 1 crore cases a year. |
| **ABV** | Alcohol by volume: the share of alcohol in the drink. | Whisky is usually around 42.8%, beer around 5%. |
| **IMFL** | Indian-made foreign liquor: spirits such as whisky, rum and vodka made in India in western styles. | Most Indian whisky brands. |
| **Country liquor** | Cheaper local spirits, sold under separate state rules. | A separate, price-led market. |
| **Excise duty** | The state tax on alcohol, often the largest part of the price. | It changes with each state's budget. |
| **Route to market** | How alcohol reaches shops in a state: through a state corporation, private distributors or auctions of shop licences. | A brand may sell to a state corporation in one state and to private wholesalers in the next. |
| **Premiumisation** | Customers moving to more expensive brands. | A drinker moving from a ₹600 to a ₹1,200 whisky. |
| **Surrogate advertising** | Advertising a brand through another product with the same name, since alcohol ads are banned. | Branded soda, music CDs or glassware ads. |

### Numbers to check

1. **Volume (cases) and value growth:** value growing faster than volume shows premiumisation.
2. **Share of premium brands (prestige and above):** where profit is made.
3. **Gross margin:** exposure to grain, molasses and glass prices.
4. **Mix of states:** dependence on states with strict pricing or high taxes.

### Questions to ask in a case

1. Which states does the company depend on, and how do they set prices and taxes?
2. Is growth coming from more drinkers, or from drinkers trading up?
3. How can the brand build awareness without direct advertising?
4. Could exports or home delivery (where states allow it) open new demand?

### Worked example: How much of a ₹1,000 bottle does the company keep?

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "The case", "icon": "fa-briefcase", "text": "A made-up whisky sells at ₹1,000 a bottle, so a case of 12 bottles costs the customer ₹12,000. We assume state taxes take 55% of the price and the trade takes 15%. The company's cost of goods is ₹1,800 a case and other costs (ads, promotion, overheads) ₹900."}
```

**Step 1, State taxes:** 55% × ₹12,000 = ₹6,600 per case.

**Step 2, Trade margins:** 15% × ₹12,000 = ₹1,800 per case.

**Step 3, Net realisation:** ₹12,000 − ₹6,600 − ₹1,800 = ₹3,600 per case.

**Step 4, Operating profit:** ₹3,600 − ₹1,800 − ₹900 = ₹900 per case, or 25% of net realisation.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "So what", "icon": "fa-flag-checkered", "text": "The company keeps only 30% of what the customer pays, and earns about ₹75 per bottle. Hence a small change in a state's tax rule can matter more than any marketing campaign, and moving drinkers up to premium brands is the most reliable way to grow profit."}
```

### Where to check the latest

- State excise department notifications and budgets
- International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI)
- Company annual reports

chapters.title: Words every industry uses
chapters.markdown:
These terms come up in almost every case, whatever the industry. Each one has a plain meaning and an example.

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Revenue** | The money a business earns from selling, before any costs. | A café's total bills for the year. |
| **EBITDA** | Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: the profit from running the business itself. | Cement and steel companies quote EBITDA per tonne. |
| **Margin** | A profit figure divided by revenue, shown as a percentage, so we can compare companies of different sizes. | An EBITDA margin of 20% means ₹20 of operating profit on every ₹100 of sales. |
| **Capacity utilisation** | How much of what a business could produce it actually produces. | A plant built for 10 lakh scooters that makes 7 lakh runs at 70%. |
| **Operating leverage** | When a large share of costs is fixed, a small rise in sales causes a big rise in profit, and the reverse. | Airlines, cement and car makers all have high operating leverage. |
| **Realisation** | The average price a company actually receives per unit, after discounts and taxes. | Net realisation per tonne of cement. |
| **Working capital** | Money tied up in running the business: stock and unpaid customer bills, minus unpaid supplier bills. | A paint company that gives dealers 60 days to pay needs more working capital. |
| **Market share** | A company's sales as a share of the whole market's sales. | If the market sells 100 cars and we sell 15, our share is 15%. |
| **Regulator** | The public body that sets the rules for an industry. | RBI for banks and NBFCs, DGCA for airlines. |

*All companies and figures in the worked examples are made up for teaching. Real company, scheme and source names appear only as public examples.*
